flashcards.q: Why isn't a bundler's code-splitting chunk boundary purely automatic for dynamically imported routes?
flashcards.a: Shared dependencies between two lazy-loaded routes force a real tradeoff: duplicate the shared module into both chunks (faster per-route initial load, wasted bytes) or extract a common chunk (no duplication, extra request/cache dependency) — a genuine tuning decision (splitChunks/manualChunks), not an automatic default.

flashcards.q: In a large multi-route app, a shared UI library re-downloads on every route navigation with no caching benefit. Likely cause?
flashcards.a: The bundler's automatic common-chunk extraction heuristic wasn't tuned for the app's actual sharing pattern, so the shared dependency is being duplicated into every route chunk instead of pulled into its own long-lived, independently-cached chunk — fix via explicit splitChunks.cacheGroups (webpack) or manualChunks (Rollup/Vite).

flashcards.q: Why do production JS bundles ship with content hashes in filenames instead of stable names?
flashcards.a: A content hash changes the filename whenever the bytes change, letting the deploy set an extremely long, aggressive cache lifetime (immutable) with zero staleness risk — a new deploy is simply a new URL, no cache invalidation needed. Stable filenames + cache-control alone create a real version-skew race during deploys.

flashcards.q: Does content-hashed asset naming eliminate version-skew risk entirely on its own?
flashcards.a: No — the entry HTML file referencing the hashed URLs must itself never be aggressively cached (Cache-Control: no-cache or very short-lived), since it's the one artifact that has to update every deploy to point at new hashes; long-lived HTML caching would serve stable HTML pointing at stale hashed assets indefinitely.
